10od2uf:364: . These two sentences characterize the essential difference between the two types of automation. Traditional software automation relies on the explicit formulation of rules—you must be able to precisely write the business logic as code. LLM automation, in contrast, relies on verifiability—you don't need to write the rules, but you must be able to judge whether the output is correct. This framework explains why LLMs have surged in capability in fields like mathematics and code, which have clear verification standards, yet fail on tasks like the "car-washing question" that humans find simple but cannot be structurally verified. It also explains the phenomenon of LLMs' "jagged intelligence." The distribution of capabilities is not smooth, but depends on which verifiable domains are covered by RL training. If a domain can be constructed with a large number of reinforcement learning samples, the model can quickly reach expert level; if it falls outside the data distribution, even if humans treat it as common sense, the model will make errors. The leap in chess ability from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 was not because "the model became generally smarter," but because someone at OpenAI decided to add chess data to pretraining.

1jlsq13:271: Karpathy's core distinction lies not in tool selection, but in the degree to which engineering discipline applies. Vibe Coding is essentially a personal developer experience with relaxed constraints—people give up direct control over code and go with the model's output, judging credibility by "feeling" rather than "verification." This is perfectly reasonable in side projects and prototype phases, because it lowers the barrier to creation. But Agentic Engineering faces professional delivery scenarios: code must be secure, behavior must be auditable, and responsibility must be assigned. Karpathy points out a key trap—when agents generate code faster and faster, teams may unconsciously skip engineering discipline, resulting in systems that "run but are unreliable." This middle layer (verification, permissions, auditing, rollback) is precisely the watershed that distinguishes amateurs from professionals.

This framework has direct practical implications: don't waste emotions on models; optimize context and reward signals instead. Karpathy says he no longer remembers API details among PyTorch, NumPy, and pandas (models remember them better than he does), but he still must understand the underlying concepts — what a tensor is, the relationship between view and storage, and when data gets copied.
